messages.text: 'State of the Game' report finds most English clubs living on financial brink

metadata.summary: The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has produced a 'State of the Game' report which has taken a forensic look at English football over the past 18 months concluding that the game's finances are dangerously exposed, with the majority of clubs living on the edge of financial disaster.
metadata.content: 'State of the Game': Independent Football Regulator's report finds most English clubs living on financial brink | Football News | Sky Sports Skip to main content 'State of the Game': Independent Football Regulator's report finds most English clubs living on financial brink Geraint Hughes Sports News Correspondent Tuesday 13 October 2026 17:02, UK The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has produced a 'State of the Game' report which has taken a forensic look at English football over the past 18 months concluding that the game's finances are dangerously exposed, with the majority of clubs living on the edge of financial disaster. The IFR added that interest and investment from around the world continues to grow within English football, but the underlying foundations of the pyramid are under intense strain and require urgent reform. Despite over £9bn generated in revenue, 94 per cent of clubs are loss-making, with long-term security being put at risk through excessive short-term spending to keep up with rivals. This, the IFR says, has led to a "dangerous cocktail of rising debt and an over-reliance on owner funding, leaving clubs and their fans at risk". Latest on YOUR PL club! Tuesday 13 October 2026 15:38, UK Image: Premier League relegation picture: Will Ipswich, Coventry and Hull all survive? Hull, Coventry and Ipswich have already collected 24 points between them after six games, so the conversation is starting to shift from pre-season vibes on whether all three newly-promoted clubs will be relegated to which established Premier League names could be in the scrap for survival. The Premier League's newly-promoted sides have often struggled to bridge the gap, with two consecutive seasons in 2023/24 and 2024/25 seeing all three newcomers relegated before Leeds and Sunderland helped buck that trend last season. metadata.summary: Paul Rowley has been confirmed as the new Castleford Tigers head coach after signing a three-year deal with the club.

Rowley left St Helens in July with the club on their way to missing out on the Super League play-offs for the first time, having previously been in charge of Salford prior to the club's financial collapse in 2025. He takes over at the Tigers following the departure of Australian Ryan Carr for personal reasons two months ago. The Brighton chairman completed a near £10m investment in the Tynecastle Park club last summer and instantly vowed to "disrupt the pattern of domination of Scottish football". At their first attempt, Hearts - who are the only team in Scotland with access to Bloom's Jamestown Analytics network - missed out on a first top-flight title since 1960 on the final day of the season. messages.text: Infantino under pressure after £1.3m US payment revealed

metadata.summary: FIFA president Gianni Infantino is under more pressure to resign after it was revealed he received £1.3m in 2024 on top of his salary.
metadata.content: Gianni Infantino: FIFA president received payment of £1.3m from World Cup company | Football News | Sky Sports Skip to main content Gianni Infantino: FIFA president received payment of £1.3m from World Cup company FIFA president Gianni Infantino has been under pressure to resign after trying to sell stakes in FIFA tournaments to private investors; he has confirmed he will stand for re-election in March 2027 as planned; financial documents reveal Infantino received undisclosed payments Kaveh Solhekol Chief Correspondent Tuesday 13 October 2026 17:03, UK Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol explains how FIFA president Gianni Infantino is under increasing pressure to resign FIFA president Gianni Infantino is under more pressure to resign after it was revealed he received £1.3m in 2024 on top of his salary. FIFA has committed to publishing Infantino's salary, bonus and allowances in its annual report every year since 2016. For 2024, he reported £3.88m ($5.1m) in salary but US tax filings show he also received £1.3m ($1.76m) from FWC2026, the company set up to organise and run this summer's World Cup, which was not publicly disclosed by FIFA in the annual report. Article 43, paragraph 13 of FIFA's statutes reads: "The individual compensation of the FIFA president, the members of the council and the FIFA secretary general shall be made public."
